1:
The chapter opens with a question, and the first thing disputed is who asks it. Ellicott weighs the prophet against Israel and prefers the prophet, explaining the unusual plural by his associating the other prophets and his own disciples with himself; the implied answer is either none or not all, and the apostle who quotes it takes the milder. Gill makes the report the gospel itself, of grace in Christ, of his person and offices and sufferings, true and yet believed by few. Clarke widens the reporters to the prophets, the Baptist, and Christ's own testimony. Henry's grief is pastoral: of the many who hear, very few believe, and ministers may complain of it to God as the prophet does.

The arm of the Lord divides them. Henry takes it for the divine power accompanying the word, made bare in the miracles that confirmed the doctrine and in its force upon the conscience; men do not perceive it because, having rebelled against the light they had, they forfeited the grace then justly withheld. Wesley identifies the arm with the Messiah, so called because the almighty power of God was seated in him, and takes revealed to mean inwardly and with power. Clarke will not have the arm here. The verb that follows needs a subject, he argues, and no arm can be said to grow up; the word differs by a letter from the one meaning seed, which elsewhere carries the promise to the patriarchs, and he reads it of Christ alone.

On the plant they agree in substance and vary in figure. Gill prefers a sucker springing from a tree's root, of which nothing is hoped, and takes the growing up for a mean entrance into the world rather than a rise to high estate. Keil and Delitzsch render it a layer-shoot and a root-sprout out of dry ground, and read the verse as looking back to how the arm of God worked in the servant's course from the first, unnoticed by those who saw the outside. Ellicott sets the picture beside the vigorous shoot from David's root and finds it reversed: the sapling is weak and frail, struggling out of dry ground. Henry supplies the history: a royal family sunk, a supposed father who was a poor carpenter, a country nothing good came from.

Whose eye watches the growth is a genuine crux. Keil and Delitzsch fix the pronoun on Jehovah, named immediately before, and reject the proposal that it looks back to the questioner, since that question's answer is nobody. Ellicott reports that some critics read before us instead, as agreeing better with the next clause, and others refer the word to the Jewish people; keeping the received text, he draws the tenderest image in the chapter, God watching this lowly growth as a mother watches her sickliest child. Wesley takes the third road: the growth was before the unbelieving Jews, who witnessed his mean original and despised him. Gill allows either the Father, in whose sight he was precious though men despised him, or the other.

Then the contempt itself. Ellicott would render the second word forsaken rather than rejected, and observes that the words for sorrow and grief imply bodily pain or disease. He calls it idle to decide beforehand whether that body could be subject to sickness, and answers that such subjection was essential to fellowship with our humanity. Keil and Delitzsch say nearly every commentator mistakes the second phrase by treating the noun as men generally, when it means men of rank. Gill hears the same, one deficient of men, with none of any figure about him but fishermen and women. Clarke notes that several ancient versions and the Jewish commentators read the next verse's stroke as leprosy. Henry adds that he was never seen to laugh, and at little over thirty was taken for nearly fifty.
4:
The turn is marked by a small particle, and Keil and Delitzsch stop over it. It may be affirmative or adversative; they choose the affirmative, since the adversative sense grows out of it and the verse's two antithetical halves carry their opposition in the pronouns. Gill reports a reading that makes it nevertheless. On the nouns there is broad agreement that they mean sickness and pain: Keil and Delitzsch render our diseases and our pains, and Ellicott says the words imply disease, which makes the evangelist's use of the verse for bodily healings legitimate. Gill reaches the same by another route, that Christ took the sinless infirmities of the nature, hunger and thirst and weariness, and healed bodies to show his sympathy and souls to show his power.

What the onlookers concluded from the suffering is the verse's other half. Wesley states it flatly: the people believed he was punished by the just judgment of God. Henry unfolds the reasoning: those justly smitten are smitten of God, so men who hated him inferred God did too, took the charges as proved, and never enquired into the merits of the cause. He sets beside it the friends who esteemed a much earlier sufferer smitten of God because his affliction was uncommon. Ellicott notes that stricken and smitten are used elsewhere specifically of leprosy and other terrible sicknesses, which is why an old Latin version renders it leprous. Clarke's contribution is textual, a well-attested pronoun that he thinks adds force to the sense and elegance to the construction.

Whether the next verse describes a life or a death is put as a question by Keil and Delitzsch and answered from the grammar. One word can be used of a man mortally wounded but not yet dead; but the forms here are pure passives denoting violence inflicted from without, and the clauses express a completed fact, so the verse speaks of the death. Ellicott says the same in a line: both words refer to the death which crowned the sufferings, and this too was vicarious. Gill guards against a narrow reading: not merely the wounds made by nails and spear but the whole of the sufferings. Wesley agrees that the word comprehends all his pains, laid on him by divine justice with his own consent.

The chastisement is read as a means rather than a quantity. Clarke reports many copies with the fuller form and renders the phrase as the chastisement by which our peace is effected, bringing us into favour with God. Ellicott takes peace in its widest sense, every form of blessing, and adds its complement, that the chastisement was an essential condition of the sufferer's perfection. Henry puts the exchange in a sentence, that Christ was in pain so that we might be at ease, and presses the healing as more than pardon: sin is not only a crime but a disease tending to the death of the soul, and the stripes purchased the grace that mortifies it.

The confession raises the question who is speaking. Gill takes the whole to be God's elect, Jew and Gentile, compared to sheep for their stupidity and their inability to return until brought back. Wesley makes it all mankind, turned in general to the way of sin and in particular to the paths different men choose. Keil and Delitzsch keep it historical, restored Israel looking back on the exile, the last state of punishment before deliverance. Ellicott takes it as both, repentant Israel and repentant humanity, and is careful about the laying on: the words state the fact of substitution without explaining it. Wesley reads the verb as making to meet, as rivers meet in the sea; Clarke as a focus, the fiery rays that should have fallen on all mankind deflected from every quarter and converged in him.
7:
Keil and Delitzsch take the first verb in its plain passive force, hard pressed, driven, hunted, and refuse a rendering that would turn the second clause into a concession, since no example exists of such a clause explaining what comes after it. Ellicott makes the second verb reflexive: he let himself be afflicted, which makes the suffering voluntarily accepted, and calls the silence that follows one of absolute acquiescence. Gill hears a legal transaction instead, rendering it that satisfaction was exacted and he answered, the surety responsible for his people, the debt paid to the last farthing and the bond cancelled. Wesley states the silence at its simplest, that he neither murmured against God nor reviled men. Ellicott adds that an earlier prophet had applied the lamb figure to himself.

The next verse begins with a phrase that can be read two ways, and Ellicott sets them out. The preposition allows taken from prison and from judgment, which many adopt as describing the iniquitous trial that preceded the death; but it allows equally through oppression and through judgment, and he prefers that, the whole procedure being tainted with iniquity. Keil and Delitzsch locate the emphasis differently: the point is not that he was taken away from suffering but that he was snatched out of the midst of it, the verb meaning hurried away rather than translated. Gill reads it all after the death, the prison being the grave, from which he was taken in a very little while and acquitted, a messenger sent to roll away the stone.

Then comes what Ellicott calls perhaps the most difficult phrase in the section. He lists the readings: who shall declare his life, the mystery of his birth; who shall count his spiritual offspring; as to his generation, meaning his contemporaries, who will consider rightly; who shall set forth that generation in its guilt. He prefers the third, since what follows names the fact they ought to have considered and did not. Wesley takes the second, the posterity being the numberless multitude who would believe, and makes the promise a reward for his willingness to be cut off. Clarke argues for the manner of life, supporting it from a rule that a crier went before a condemned man inviting anyone who knew of his innocence to speak, a benefit no one offered at this trial.

The burial produces the sharpest division in the chapter. Gill takes the fulfilment as commonly told, and observes that the clauses fit exactly if transposed, the grave made with the rich and the death with the wicked; failing that, both classes were concerned about the tomb, two rich men taking the body down and soldiers set to guard it. Ellicott refuses the whole approach. It requires inverting the clauses, introduces a note out of keeping with the description, and breaks the parallelism, which requires the rich of one line to answer the wicked of the other and so to mean the wrongfully rich. On his reading men assigned him not the burial of a saint but that of an oppressor whom nobody lamented.

Ellicott presses on: the clause should read although and not because, since because assumes the honourable burial the words are supposed to imply, and he doubts whether a clandestine funeral without public mourning would adequately recognise the victim's holiness. Clarke goes the other way with an antiquarian argument, taking a disputed word as a noun meaning heights, since the oldest tombs were mounds of heaped earth often crowned with a pillar and Jewish graves were set on eminences, so that his high place easily means his tomb. Keil and Delitzsch worry only about who assigns it, settling on his generation rather than God or the people. Wesley notes that he made his grave because the yielding was his own act, and that with the wicked means sameness of condition, not place.
10:
The last movement names the agent, and they differ on how far to press it. Ellicott refers the sufferings not to chance or fate or even the wickedness of the persecutors but to the absolute good pleasure of the Father, showing itself most fully in the hour of apparent failure. Wesley distinguishes causes: God the principal cause, men's sins the deserving one. Gill goes furthest: when the sins of his people were laid on him the wrath of God came upon him for them, and the sufferings were not merely permitted but predetermined and in a manner delighted in. Henry draws a line exactly there. Scripture nowhere says that Christ in his sufferings underwent the wrath of God, he insists; it says the Lord bruised him, awakened his own sword against him, and put the bitter cup into his hand.

The next clause is conditional, and its grammar contested. Ellicott would render it if his soul shall make a trespass offering, he will see his seed, and insists on the term: the trespass offering was distinct from the sin offering, involving a confession of guilt and a payment assessed by the priest, so carrying the idea not of atonement only but of satisfaction proportioned to the sin. Keil and Delitzsch render it much the same, if his soul would pay a trespass-offering. Clarke reports a copy permitting a passive, if his soul shall be made an offering, which some Greek witnesses support. Wesley alone keeps the received text's second person, God addressed directly as the one who makes his Son a sacrifice.

The promises divide over who receives them. Wesley takes the prolonging simply: he shall live and reign with God for ever. Henry keeps the family image: many who see their children's children are content to depart, but this one will not commit so numerous a household to another. He notes that some refer the clause to believers, whose seed endures. Clarke takes that road openly, reading it of the spiritual progeny rather than the person, so that the promise is that Christianity shall endure to the end of time; and he adds a claim of his own, that every succeeding century has witnessed more of it than the one before. Gill keeps the satisfaction personal, the fruit seen with inexpressible pleasure.

How the servant sees and is satisfied turns on a preposition. Keil and Delitzsch canvass a local sense, far from the trouble, and a temporal one, immediately after it, before settling on the causal. Ellicott renders it on account of the travail of his soul he shall see and be refreshed, and finds the truest illustration in the promise made to the dying thief. Gill notes a rendering making it seeing himself freed from trouble. The knowledge in the next clause admits an objective and a subjective sense, and Ellicott, judging each true, is glad the prophet used a phrase holding both, though he leans to the servant's own knowledge; Wesley takes it flatly as the knowledge of him. Clarke would drop the word righteous as a copyist's repetition overloading the line.

The reward is a portion among the great, and here too a rival rendering offers. Ellicott takes the great and the powerful for the kings and rulers of mankind, with whom the once forsaken servant takes his place, though not by their means; he records that the ancient versions and some moderns read instead that the multitude is given him as a prey, and Keil and Delitzsch report the same. Gill is drawn to it, the Lord's people being his portion. Clarke presses the many of the last verses to their widest, the multitudes made sinners by one offence, and finds the intercession fulfilled in the prayer from the cross. Henry notes the aggravation of his being executed between two malefactors, as if the worst of the three.
